376: "Star of descending night! Fair is your light in the west!
You lift your unshorn head from your cloud; your steps are stately on your hill.
What do you behold on the plain?
The murmur of the torrent comes from far off.
Roaring waves climb the distant rock.
The flies of evening are on their feeble wings; the hum of their course is on the field.
What do you behold, fair light?
The waves come with joy around you; they bathe your lovely hair.
Let the light of Ossian's soul arise!
377: "And it does arise in its strength!
Their gathering is on Lora, as in the days of other years.
Fingal comes like a watery column of mist; his heroes are around him.
And see the bards of song — gray-haired Ullin, stately Ryno,
Alpin with the tuneful voice, and the soft complaint of Minona!
How you are changed, my friends, since the days of Selma's feast — when we contended like the gales of spring as they fly along the hill and bend by turns the feebly whistling grass.
378: "Minona came forth in her beauty, with downcast look and tearful eye.
Her hair flew slowly in the blast that rushed at intervals from the hill.
The souls of the heroes were sad when she raised her tuneful voice.
Often had they seen the grave of Salgar, the dark dwelling of white-bosomed Colma.
Colma, left alone on the hill with all her voice of song!
Salgar promised to come — but the night came down around her.
Hear the voice of Colma, as she sat alone on the hill!
379: It is night; I am alone, forlorn on the hill of storms.
The wind is heard on the mountain.
The torrent is howling down the rock.
No hut shelters me from the rain — forlorn on the hill of winds!
380: Lead me, some light, to the place where my love rests alone from the chase!
His bow beside him unstrung, his dogs panting around him.
But here I must sit alone by the rock of the mossy stream.
The stream and the wind roar aloud.
I do not hear the voice of my love.
Why does my Salgar delay? Why does the chief of the hill break his promise?
Here is the rock, and here the tree! Here is the roaring stream!
You promised to be here with the night.
Ah, where has my Salgar gone?
With you I would fly from my father, with you from my brother of pride.
Our families have long been enemies — but we are not enemies, O Salgar!
381: "Cease a little while, O wind! Stream, be silent awhile!
Let my voice be heard around; let my wanderer hear me!
Salgar, it is Colma who calls.
Here is the tree and the rock.
Salgar, my love, I am here!
Why do you delay your coming?
See, the calm moon comes forth.
The flood is bright in the valley.
The rocks are gray on the steep.
I do not see him on the brow of the hill.
His dogs do not come before him with word that he is near.
382: "Who lie on the heath beside me?
Are they my love and my brother?
Speak to me, O my friends!
To Colma they give no reply.
Speak to me: I am alone!
My soul is tormented with fears.
Ah, they are dead!
Their swords are red from the fight.
O my brother, my brother, why have you slain my Salgar?
Why, O Salgar, have you slain my brother?
Dear were you both to me! What shall I say in your praise?
You were fair on the hill among thousands; he was terrible in fight.
Speak to me! Hear my voice! Hear me, sons of my love!
They are silent — silent for ever!
Cold, cold are their breasts of clay!
Oh, from the rock on the hill, from the top of the windy steep, speak, you ghosts of the dead!
Speak — I will not be afraid!
Where have you gone to rest?
In what cave of the hill shall I find the departed?
No feeble voice is on the gale, no answer half drowned in the storm.
383: "I sit in my grief; I wait for morning in my tears.
Raise the tomb, you friends of the dead.
Do not close it until Colma comes.
My life flies away like a dream.
Here I shall rest with my friends, by the stream of the sounding rock.
When night comes on the hill, when the loud winds rise, my ghost shall stand in the blast and mourn the death of my friends.
The hunter shall hear me from his hut; he shall fear my voice, but love it.
For sweet shall my voice be for my friends — pleasant were her friends to Colma.
384: "Such was your song, Minona, softly blushing daughter of Torman.
Our tears fell for Colma, and our souls were sad.
Ullin came with his harp; he gave us the song of Alpin.
The voice of Alpin was pleasant, the soul of Ryno was a beam of fire.
But they had gone to rest in the narrow house; their voices had ceased in Selma.
Ullin had returned one day from the chase before the heroes fell.
He heard their strife on the hill; their song was soft, but sad.
They mourned the fall of Morar, first of mortal men.
His soul was like the soul of Fingal, his sword like the sword of Oscar.
But he fell, and his father mourned; his sister's eyes were full of tears.
Minona's eyes were full of tears — the sister of car-borne Morar.
She withdrew from the song of Ullin, like the moon in the west when she foresees the shower and hides her fair head in a cloud.
I touched the harp with Ullin; the song of morning rose.
385: The wind and the rain are past; calm is the noon of day.
The clouds are divided in heaven.
Over the green hills flies the inconstant sun.
Red through the stony valley comes down the stream of the hill.
Sweet are your murmurs, O stream — but sweeter still is the voice I hear.
It is the voice of Alpin, the son of song, mourning for the dead.
Bent is his head with age, red his tearful eye.
Alpin, son of song, why alone on the silent hill?
Why do you lament, like a blast in the wood, like a wave on the lonely shore?
386: My tears, O Ryno, are for the dead; my voice for those who have passed away.
Tall you are on the hill, fair among the sons of the valley.
But you shall fall like Morar, and the mourner shall sit on your tomb.
The hills shall know you no more; your bow shall lie unstrung in your hall.
387: "You were swift, O Morar, as a roe on the desert, terrible as a meteor of fire.
Your wrath was as the storm.
Your sword in battle was as lightning in the field.
Your voice was as a stream after rain, like thunder on distant hills.
Many fell by your arm; they were consumed in the flames of your wrath.
But when you returned from war, how peaceful was your brow.
Your face was like the sun after rain, like the moon in the silence of night, calm as the breast of the lake when the loud wind is laid.
388: "Narrow is your dwelling now; dark the place of your abode.
With three steps I compass your grave, O you who were once so great!
Four stones with their heads of moss are the only memorial of you.
A tree with scarcely a leaf, and long grass whistling in the wind, mark for the hunter's eye the grave of the mighty Morar.
Morar, you are laid low indeed.
You have no mother to mourn you, no maid with her tears of love.
Dead is she who brought you into the world.
Fallen is the daughter of Morglan.
389: Who is this whose head is white with age, whose eyes are red with tears, who trembles at every step?
It is your father, O Morar — the father of no son but you.
He heard of your fame in war, he heard of enemies scattered.
He heard of Morar's renown — why did he not hear of his wound?
Weep — but your son does not hear you.
Deep is the sleep of the dead, low their pillow of dust.
No more shall he hear your voice, no more wake at your call.
When shall it be morning in the grave, to bid the sleeper wake?
Farewell, bravest of men, conqueror in the field!
But the field shall see you no more, nor the dark wood be lightened with the splendour of your steel.
The song shall preserve your name.
Future times shall hear of you — they shall hear of the fallen Morar.
390: "The grief of all arose, but most of all the bursting sigh of Armin.
He remembers the death of his son, who fell in the days of his youth.
Carmor was near the hero, the chief of the echoing Galmal.
Why does Armin sigh so? he said.
The song comes with its music to melt and please the soul.
It is like soft mist that rises from a lake and pours over the silent valley; the green flowers fill with dew, but the sun comes back in his strength, and the mist is gone.
Why are you sad, O Armin, chief of sea-surrounded Gorma?
391: "Sad I am, and my cause of grief is not small.
Carmor, you have lost no son; you have lost no daughter of beauty.
Colgar the valiant lives, and Annira, fairest of maidens.
The branches of your house rise, O Carmor — but Armin is the last of his race.
Dark is your bed, O Daura; deep your sleep in the tomb.
When will you wake with your songs, with all your voice of music?
392: "Arise, winds of autumn, arise! Blow along the heath.
Streams of the mountains, roar! Roar, tempests, in the groves of my oaks!
Walk through the broken clouds, O moon; show your pale face at intervals.
Bring back to my mind the night when all my children fell — when Arindal the mighty fell, when Daura the lovely failed.
Daura, my daughter, you were fair — fair as the moon on Fura, white as the driven snow, sweet as the breathing gale.
Arindal, your bow was strong, your spear was swift on the field, your look was like mist on the wave, your shield a red cloud in a storm.
Armar, renowned in war, came and sought Daura's love.
He was not long refused; fair was the hope of their friends.
393: "Erath, son of Odgal, resented it: his brother had been slain by Armar.
He came disguised as a son of the sea; fair was his boat on the wave, white his locks of age, calm his serious brow.
Fairest of women, he said, lovely daughter of Armin — a rock not far off in the sea bears a tree on its side, and the fruit shines red from afar.
I come to carry his love to him.
She went; she called on Armar.
Nothing answered but the son of the rock.
Armar, my love, my love! Why do you torment me with fear?
Hear, son of Arnart, hear! It is Daura who calls you.
Erath the traitor fled laughing to the land.
She lifted up her voice; she called for her brother and her father.
Arindal! Armin! Is there none to help you, Daura?
394: Arindal, my son, came down from the hill, rough with the spoils of the chase.
His arrows rattled at his side, his bow was in his hand, and five dark-gray dogs followed his steps.
He saw fierce Erath on the shore; he seized him and bound him to an oak.
Thick wound the thongs of hide around his limbs, and he loaded the winds with his groans.
Arindal put out on the deep in his boat to bring Daura to land.
Armar came in his wrath and let fly the gray-feathered shaft.
It sang, it sank in your heart, O Arindal, my son — for Erath the traitor you died.
The oar stopped at once; he gasped on the rock, and died.
What was your grief, O Daura, when your brother's blood was poured around your feet!
The boat is broken in two.
Armar plunges into the sea to rescue his Daura, or to die.
A sudden blast from the hill came over the waves; he sank, and rose no more.
395: "Alone on the sea-beaten rock, my daughter was heard to lament; her cries were frequent and loud.
All night I stood on the shore; I saw her by the faint beam of the moon.
All night I heard her cries.
Loud was the wind; the rain beat hard on the hill.
Before morning came her voice grew weak; it died away like the evening breeze among the grass of the rocks.
Spent with grief, she died, and left you, Armin, alone.
Gone is my strength in war, fallen my pride among women.
When the storms rise aloft, when the north lifts the wave on high, I sit by the sounding shore and look at the fatal rock.
396: "Often by the setting moon I see the ghosts of my children; half unseen, they walk together in mournful conference."
397: A torrent of tears streaming from Charlotte's eyes, and relieving her bursting heart, stopped Werther's recitation.
He threw down the book, seized her hand, and wept bitterly.
Charlotte leaned on her hand and buried her face in her handkerchief; the agitation of both was extreme.
They felt that their own fate was pictured in the misfortunes of Ossian's heroes — they felt it together, and their tears redoubled.
Werther rested his forehead on Charlotte's arm; she trembled and wished to be gone, but sorrow and sympathy lay like a leaden weight on her soul.
She recovered herself shortly, and begged Werther through broken sobs to leave her, imploring him with the utmost earnestness to do as she asked.
He trembled; his heart was ready to burst.
Then, taking up the book again, he began to read once more, in a voice broken by sobs.
398: "Why do you wake me, O spring?
Your voice woos me, saying: I refresh you with the dews of heaven.
But the time of my decay is near, and the storm is at hand that shall wither my leaves.
Tomorrow the traveller will come — he will come who saw me in my beauty; his eye will search the field for me, and he will not find me."
399: The whole force of these words fell on the unfortunate Werther.
Full of despair, he threw himself at Charlotte's feet, seized her hands, and pressed them to his eyes and to his forehead.
A sense of his fatal purpose struck her now for the first time.
Her senses were bewildered; she held his hands, pressed them to her breast, and, leaning toward him in the tenderest pity, her warm cheek touched his.
They lost sight of everything.
The world disappeared from their eyes.
He clasped her in his arms, strained her to his breast, and covered her trembling lips with passionate kisses.
"Werther!" she cried in a faint voice, turning away. "Werther!"
And with a feeble hand she pushed him from her.
At length, in the firm voice of virtue, she exclaimed, "Werther!"
He did not resist, but tore himself from her arms and fell on his knees before her.
Charlotte rose, and in disordered grief, in mingled tones of love and resentment, she cried, "It is the last time, Werther!"
"You shall never see me again!"
Then, casting one last tender look at her unfortunate lover, she rushed into the next room and locked the door.
Werther held out his arms, but did not dare to hold her back.
He stayed on the ground with his head resting on the sofa for half an hour, until a noise brought him to his senses.
The servant came in.
He then walked up and down the room; and when he was alone again, he went to Charlotte's door and said in a low voice, "Charlotte, Charlotte! Only one word more, one last adieu!"
She gave no answer.
He stopped, and listened, and entreated; but all was silent.
At length he tore himself from the place, crying, "Adieu, Charlotte, adieu for ever!"
